title: Making beeswax candles
subtitle: Dipped, rolled, and moulded candles from rendered wax.
excerpt: Beeswax candles are a practical use for cappings wax and old comb from the hive. They burn longer and cleaner than paraffin, and the natural honey scent needs no added fragrance. There are three main methods: dipped tapers, rolled sheets, and poured moulds. Each needs rendered, filtered wax to produce a clean result.
sourceNotes: Vivienne Munn, The Beekeeper's Bible (2010), wax chapter. BBKA, Using Beeswax (2021). Joanna Ryde, Candle-making with Natural Waxes (2019).

glossaryTerms.definition: Melting raw cappings or old comb and straining out debris and dead bees to produce clean, usable wax.
Choosing a wick thickness matched to the candle diameter. A too-thin wick tunnels; a too-thick wick produces excessive soot.

content.text: Before making candles, the wax must be rendered and filtered. Raw cappings and old comb contain propolis, cocoon fragments, and debris that produce dark, grainy candles if not removed.
cappings and old comb by melting slowly in a double boiler (a bowl over a pot of hot water). Do not melt wax in direct contact with a hob flame; it is highly flammable above 200 C.
Pour the melted wax through a double layer of muslin cloth into a clean container. The cloth retains debris. Wax at 70 to 80 C pours freely; cooler wax becomes too viscous to filter.
Allow to solidify. Impurities often settle to the bottom; slice off the dark layer from the underside of the finished block before using for candles.

Rolled beeswax candles use pre-made honeycomb-embossed wax sheets available from beekeeping suppliers. They require no heat, just a warm room. Roll the sheet tightly around a length of wicking, keeping the wick centred and the roll even. The candle is ready to use immediately. This is the fastest method and produces a reliable result.
Melt rendered wax in a tall, deep container (at least 25 cm deep for a 20 cm taper). Keep wax at 70 to 75 C throughout dipping.

Prime the wick by dipping once and letting it harden fully (2 to 3 minutes). Then begin layering by dipping, withdrawing, and allowing 30 to 60 seconds between dips. Each dip adds a thin layer. 20 to 30 dips produces a candle of good weight.
Hang or stand finished tapers to cool straight. A bent taper can be gently straightened immediately after the final dip by rolling on a flat board while still warm.

Pour rendered wax at 70 C into a wicked mould. Thread the wick through the mould base before pouring. Beeswax shrinks as it cools and pulls away from the sides of the mould; a small depression usually forms at the top after the first pour. Top up with a second pour to keep the surface flat.

for beeswax: candles under 30 mm diameter use a 2/0 or 3/0 square-braid cotton wick. Candles 30 to 50 mm use a 1/0 or #1. Candles over 50 mm may need a #2 or #3. Burn a test candle for 2 hours before committing to a large batch; if the wax pool barely reaches the edge of the candle, go up a size.

attrs.cue: Finished candle has a grainy, frosted surface
attrs.cause: Wax poured too cool, or water contamination in the wax
attrs.fix: Pour at 68 to 72 C. Ensure all rendering equipment was completely dry before use. Grainy candles burn normally; the appearance is cosmetic.

attrs.cue: Taper candles drip excessively when burning
attrs.cause: Wick too thick, or taper was cooled too slowly and the layers did not bond
attrs.fix: Try a smaller wick size. For dipped tapers, ensure each layer has cooled to the touch before the next dip.
